title: Milestone: Inside the Mind
objective: After this level you can connect perception, learning, memory, motivation and emotion into one picture of how experience becomes action.
summary: Halfway there, the pieces connect: attention and memory filter and rebuild experience, rewards shape habits, and a judgment plus a body state becomes an emotion.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Follow one moment from feeling to action.
cards.body: Your teacher asks you to give a talk to the class. In a moment your mind judges the situation, your body reacts, a feeling arrives, and you want to do something about it. Two students can get the same request and feel completely different. Five chapters gave you the pieces; here they are in one chain.

cards.headline: Four parts of one emotion
cards.body: Psychologists describe an emotion as four things at once: what you feel inside, how you show it, how you appraise the situation, and how your body responds. In appraisal theory, that judgment comes first and steers the feeling. One student sees a chance to shine and feels happy; another dreads public speaking and feels uneasy. Same event, different judgment, different emotion.

items.label: Before the feeling
points: Your judgment of the event shapes what you feel
Two people can feel differently about the same event

items.label: The feeling
points: Two-factor view: arousal plus a label from the situation
Intense and about something, unlike a longer, milder mood

items.label: After the feeling
points: Drives push to restore balance; incentives pull
What ends a drive tends to become a habit

cards.headline: Milestone: inside the mind
learned: How perception, attention and memory decide what you notice, what you keep and what you rebuild.
Why psychologists study an unseen mind through behavior, body signals and self-reports.
How rewards, repetition and watching others shape habits, and when a promised prize kills the fun.
How a judgment and a body state become an emotion, and why some famous findings shrank on retest.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap: why can two students feel differently about the same request to give a talk?

options.label: Only one of them has a body that reacts
options.rationale: Both have bodily responses.

options.label: Emotions come before any judgment is made
options.rationale: In appraisal theory, the judgment comes first.

options.label: They judge the moment differently, and that shapes the feeling
Moods and emotions are exactly the same thing
options.rationale: Moods are longer and milder than emotions.

questions.explanation: In appraisal theory, your judgment of an event comes first and shapes the emotion, so the same request can bring happiness or unease.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap, from Level 1: nobody can read another person's mind. So how do psychologists study it?

options.label: By trusting their own introspection as the final word
options.rationale: Wundt's trained observers kept disagreeing.

options.label: By measuring behavior, body signals and self-reports, then inferring
By studying only animals and never asking people
options.rationale: Self-reports from people are one of the main measures.

options.label: By waiting for a machine that reads thoughts directly
options.rationale: They work indirectly, from what they can observe.

questions.explanation: Psychologists measure what they can observe, such as behavior, biological signals and self-reports, and infer from those what the mind is doing.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap: what do Chapter 2's attention and Chapter 4's working memory have in common?

options.label: Both take in everything the senses collect
options.rationale: Attention selects a little from a lot.

options.label: Both grow without limit with enough practice
options.rationale: Chunking packs more into each slot, but the slots stay few.

options.label: Both keep what they hold for a lifetime
options.rationale: That's long-term memory, not attention or working memory.

options.label: Both handle only a small amount at a time

questions.explanation: Attention can take in only a small amount of information at a time, and working memory holds about 4 chunks.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap, from Level 27: why do people keep pulling a slot machine long after it stops paying?

options.label: Behavior rewarded now and then lasts longer once rewards stop
The machine pays on a fixed, predictable schedule
options.rationale: Slots pay after an unpredictable number of pulls.

options.label: Each pull is punished, which makes pulling likelier
options.rationale: Punishment makes a behavior less likely.

options.label: Every pull pays a little, so the habit stays strong
options.rationale: Behavior rewarded every time fades faster once rewards stop.

questions.explanation: Most gambling pays on a variable ratio schedule, and behavior rewarded only some of the time keeps going longest after rewards stop.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap, from Levels 37 and 38: how can a question asked after an event change a witness's memory of it?

options.label: The memory is sealed at once, so it can't change
options.rationale: Recall rebuilds a memory, so it can change.

options.label: Recall rebuilds the event, and new details get built in
The question erases the memory and leaves a blank
options.rationale: Details get added, not just lost.

options.label: Only memories from early childhood can be changed
options.rationale: Students' memories of a film changed within a week.

questions.explanation: Remembering is reconstruction, so misleading information met after an event can blend into the memory, like broken glass that was never there.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap: Thorndike's law of effect says rewarded behavior gets repeated. Why did children promised a Good Player Award later draw less?

options.label: The award felt like a punishment for drawing badly
options.rationale: It was a prize; expecting it was what mattered.

options.label: Any reward, even a surprise one, cuts interest
options.rationale: Surprise awards left interest intact.

options.label: They had never enjoyed drawing in the first place
options.rationale: They already loved drawing with markers.

options.label: The expected prize crowded out their own reason to draw

questions.explanation: In the overjustification effect, an expected, tangible reward can shrink the inside reason for an activity, so effort starts to depend on the prize.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap, from Level 44: willpower was pictured as a battery that runs down. What did the 2016 test in 23 labs find?

options.label: An effect near zero
A much larger effect than in 1998
options.rationale: It found almost none.

options.label: An effect only in people who ate radishes twice
options.rationale: Radishes were the 1998 task.

options.label: That willpower recharges after exactly an hour
options.rationale: The study made no such claim.

questions.explanation: The 2016 multi-lab replication, with 2,141 people in 23 labs, found an ego-depletion effect near zero.
